input:
In recent years, the conversion of carbon dioxide into useful chemical products has attracted considerable attention, and the reaction of carbon dioxide with hydrogen over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to produce dimethyl ether is an interesting route that has been the subject of ongoing investigation. In this study, two different forms of the catalyst, namely a washcoated monolith catalyst and an extruded pellet catalyst, were tested and compared under identical conditions in order to assess their relative performance. Space-time yield, which is a key performance indicator in this context, is defined as the mass of product obtained per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). The tests were carried out at 230 °C and 60 bar, with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and a single feed composition throughout.

Turning to the results, the washcoated monolith catalyst achieved a space-time yield of 1.04 kg L-1 h-1, with a pressure drop of 0.25 bar and an activity loss of 6% after 100 h on stream. The extruded pellet catalyst, by comparison, delivered a space-time yield of 0.46 kg L-1 h-1, with a pressure drop of 1.3 bar and an activity loss of 18% after 100 h. Overall, the monolith therefore appears to offer a considerably more favourable combination of performance characteristics, delivering the higher yield while at the same time imposing the lower pressure drop and retaining its activity noticeably better over the duration of the test. It is worth adding that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested in this work, and that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported together for the same catalyst charge in the wider literature.
target:
Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give dimethyl ether. Two forms of the catalyst, a washcoated monolith and an extruded pellet, are compared at one feed composition. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1).

Both catalysts were tested at 230 °C and 60 bar with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3. The washcoated monolith gave a space-time yield of 1.04 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 0.25 bar, and an activity loss of 6% after 100 h. The extruded pellet gave a space-time yield of 0.46 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 1.3 bar, and an activity loss of 18% after 100 h.

The monolith leads on all three measures at the tested conditions: the higher yield, the lower pressure drop, and the smaller activity loss over the same test duration. The comparison is a comparison of catalyst form at fixed chemistry and fixed conditions, and the margins are large enough that the ranking does not rest on any single measure.

Each measure answers a different design question, and the three are stated together because a catalyst is chosen on the three together. Space-time yield sets the catalyst volume a duty requires. Pressure drop sets the cost of passing the feed through that volume, paid as compression or as pumping. Activity loss sets how long the charge holds its initial performance before the yield figures above cease to describe it. A form that led on yield alone, at a heavy pressure drop or with a fast loss of activity, would present a genuine trade-off; at the tested conditions no trade-off arises, because the same form leads on all three.

The claim is limited to the tested scope. One feed composition was tested, and no sulfur-bearing feed was tested, so behaviour on sulfur-bearing feeds is outside the claim. Yield and pressure drop, reported here for the same catalyst charge, are seldom reported together in the literature, and the comparison with other catalysts is limited accordingly.
